t: This is RAAV, Robot As A Verifier.
Give it a prototype and its manual and a low-cost robot arm tests
every control it can find then reports what it measured.
Here it is on our centrifuge.
It scans the panel with one wrist camera and finds six controls.
We give it the order of steps, a model writes the plan quoting the manual for
what each step should do, and a person approves it before anything moves.
Then the arm works through it.
It loads a test tube, closes the lid, switches the power on,
presses TIME, turns the speed dial, and presses START, then STOP.
A board inside the centrifuge reports what each control actually
did, and fixed rules turn that into a verdict.
All five controls it pressed responded, but two results didn't add up.
TIME didn't add any time, and after START the display read LID instead of running.
RAAV suspected the tube, which had let go well above its seat
and flagged both for a person to check instead of guessing.
A tube that won't seat is a fault our CAD agent has fixed before in simulation.
It widened the adapter's bore and added a lead-in, and on retest the tube seated.
Our microwave's hinge fused shut when printed, its second revision
opens the clearances, and hinges are for the next agent.
Under the hood, RAAV is two systems.
System 1 is the robot.
Perception, motion, force limits, and the verdict rules.
System 2 is a frontier model that plans, recovers
from failed steps, and diagnoses causes.
Between them is a set of tools, none of which moves a motor or
grades a step, so either side can be swapped and abstracted.
Any of four models, the simulator, or the real arm.
Vision-language models fold all of this into one network and need
new demonstrations for every task, but our split just needs a manual
due to the unparalleled capabilities of frontier models.
Why does this matter?
Software already has verification, from AI-written proofs
to flight code, and hardware has nothing like it.
In James Dyson's words, I made 5,127 prototypes of my vacuum before I got it right.
There were 5,126 failures.
Important fields like biosafety and space development tell the same story.
In hardware, failures surface late.
Today, RAAV runs on 12 appliance designs in simulation and
a real centrifuge and microwave with its planner in the cloud,
and any lab with a low-cost arm could do the same.
As AI starts designing hardware and iterating in the auto-research loop of the
physical world, every design should be measured before anyone relies on it.
That's RAAV.
